summary: Describes a protocol, building on RFC 4819, for provisioning keys and certificates to a server using SSH transport, with keys organized into namespaces that can serve applications such as SSH, KMIP and SNMP. It is an informational description of a vendor-specific design.

eli5.summary: A safe way to put keys on a server and sort them into labeled boxes.

questions: ssh public key subsystem for certificates
subtitle: Organize keys and certificates in namespaces over SSH.

tldr.problem: The original SSH Public Key Subsystem (RFC 4819) provisions keys to a server but lacks a way to organize them by application or service.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds namespaces to group keys and certificates by their purpose (e.g., 'ssh', 'ssl', 'kmip') and provides new operations to add, remove, and list certificates in specific namespaces.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now manage keys and certificates for multiple applications through a single protocol, with per-namespace access control. The design is backward compatible with RFC 4819 version 2.

today: RFC 7076 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It describes a vendor-specific extension to RFC 4819 that remains available for use by implementations that need key organization by namespace.

sections.title: Introduction to the Extension
sections.content:
The Secure Shell (SSH) Public Key Subsystem, defined in RFC 4819, provides a way to upload and manage a user's public keys on an SSH server. This document describes an extension to that protocol, adding a namespace concept that lets clients organize keys and certificates by the application or service that will use them.

P6R's extension runs as an SSH subsystem named publickey@p6r.com and operates on top of the SSH transport layer. Keys and certificates can be used for client authentication or to encrypt responses back to the client. The namespace system allows a single server to use the same key distribution protocol for different applications like SSH, KMIP, SNMP, or SSL, each with its own namespace.

The protocol is designed to be backward compatible with RFC 4819 version 2 while introducing version 3 with the new capabilities.
sections.eli5: SSH lets you send keys to a server. This adds labels (namespaces) so a server can keep different types of keys separate.

sections.title: Core Extensions
sections.content:
Three main extensions are added to the original protocol. First, a new set of status codes are defined: SSH_PUBLICKEY_CERTIFICATE_NOT_FOUND (192), SSH_PUBLICKEY_CERTIFICATE_NOT_SUPPORTED (193), SSH_PUBLICKEY_CERTIFICATE_ALREADY_PRESENT (194), SSH_PUBLICKEY_ACTION_NOT_AUTHORIZED (195), and SSH_PUBLICKEY_CANNOT_CREATE_NAMESPACE (196). These allow the server to report specific failure reasons in machine-readable form.

Second, a version packet starts every connection, letting both sides declare which protocol version they support. This document defines version 3.

Third, a namespace attribute is added to all operations. A namespace is a UTF-8 string of up to 300 characters that groups keys and certificates. The default namespace is ssh when none is provided. By convention, protocol namespaces use lowercase abbreviations (e.g., ssl, kmip, snmp), while application namespaces include the product and vendor name.
sections.eli5: The extension adds version numbers so client and server agree on what they support, error codes so the server can explain what went wrong, and namespace names so everything knows which box to use.

sections.title: Certificate Operations
sections.content:
The protocol adds four new operations for working with certificates. Add-certificate uploads a certificate in formats such as X.509, pgp-sign-rsa, or pgp-sign-dss, with a namespace attribute telling the server which namespace to store it in. If the namespace does not exist, the server creates it (unless the user lacks permission). The operation can overwrite an existing certificate or reject if one already exists.

Remove-certificate deletes a certificate from a namespace by its format and blob. List-certificates queries the server and returns all certificates in a namespace, zero or more at a time, ending with a status packet. List-namespaces shows all namespaces visible to the authenticated user; the server may hide namespaces the user is not authorized to access.

All certificate operations require the namespace attribute. Only one namespace can be specified per request. A user can upload the same certificate to multiple namespaces by sending separate requests.
sections.eli5: You can add a certificate to a box, remove one, see all certificates in a box, or ask which boxes exist. Each action needs to say which box to use.

sections.title: Extended Public Key Operations
sections.content:
The protocol also extends the original RFC 4819 public key operations. Add now optionally accepts a namespace attribute, allowing a public key to be saved to a specific namespace instead of just the default. If the namespace does not exist, the server creates it. An attribute system allows metadata to be attached to keys.

Remove now accepts attributes and can specify a namespace from which to delete a public key. List also accepts attributes and an optional namespace parameter to query public keys from a specific namespace. Server responses may include the namespace attribute so the client knows which namespace each key is in.

Unlike certificate operations, the namespace attribute is optional for public key operations, allowing backward compatibility with servers that do not understand namespaces.
sections.eli5: The original way to add and remove keys gets updated to work with boxes too, but without requiring them so that old servers still work.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Deployment
sections.content:
The protocol assumes it runs over a secure, authenticated SSH channel, protecting it from network-level attacks. The server implementation must enforce access controls to restrict what each user can do in each namespace. For example, one user might be able to list a namespace's keys but not add or remove them. If a user's action violates the server's access policy, the server returns SSH_PUBLICKEY_ACTION_NOT_AUTHORIZED.

Implementation correctness is critical. If a server incorrectly handles attributes attached to keys and certificates, it could authorize access that was not intended or apply fewer restrictions than desired. The protocol relies on correct server behavior and places the responsibility for access control on the server implementation, not the protocol itself.

Because the protocol is informational and vendor-specific, IANA registration is not required for the new status codes, which fall in the Private Use range of the SSH Public Key Subsystem registry.
sections.eli5: The server has to be trusted to keep its boxes locked properly, and if it makes a mistake, keys could end up in the wrong hands.
